On the minimal normal compactification

of a polynomial in two variables

Angelo Vistoli**Partially supported by the University of Bologna, funds for selected research topics.

Dipartimento di Matematica

Università di Bologna

Piazza di Porta San Donato 5

40127 Bologna, Italy

E-mail address: vistoli@dm.unibo.it

1 Introduction

Let CC be an integral affine curve over a field κ\kappa, α,β:C↪𝐀2\alpha,\beta:C\hookrightarrow{\bf A}^{2} two closed embeddings. We say that α\alpha and β\beta are equivalent when there is an automorphism ϕ\phi of 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} with ϕ∘α=β\phi\circ\alpha=\beta. It was stated by B. Segre ([Se]) and proved by Suzuki in [Su] that when κ=𝐂\kappa={\bf C} any embedding of 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} into 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} is equivalent to the standard embedding t↦(t,0)t\mapsto(t,0). This was generalized to the case that κ\kappa is arbitrary, and the degree of ff is prime to the characteristic of κ\kappa, by Abhyankar and Moh ([AM]). This is what is usually called the Abhyankar–Moh theorem. On the other hand, there are many affine curves with an infinite number of non equivalent embeddings into 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2}: for example, 𝐀1∖{0}{\bf A}^{1}\setminus\{0\}.

Suzuki in [Su] also proves a very nice result: if CC is smooth and has only one branch at infinity (that is, it is the complement of a point in a smooth projective curve) and ff is a generator of the ideal of CC in 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2}, then CC is an ordinary fiber of ff, that is, ff is a topological fibration in a neighborhood of 0. In their important, and arduous, article [AS] Abhyankar and Singh carry the study of this case much further, over arbitrary fields; in particular, for example, such a curve CC has at most finitely many nonequivalent embeddings, with appropriate conditions on the characteristic of the field.

Another proof of Suzuki’s theorem was given by Artal Bartolo, in [AB], based on the results of [EN], relating knot theory with the theory of polynomials in two variables.

Now, let f:𝐀2→𝐀1f\colon{\bf A}^{2}\to{\bf A}^{1} be a polynomial in two variables defined over an algebraically closed field κ\kappa. We shall always assume that ff is primitive, that is, that the generic fiber of ff is integral. We consider the minimal normal compactification f¯:X→𝐀1\overline{f}\colon X\to{\bf A}^{1} of ff, namely the only normal irreducible surface XX containing 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} as an open subset, together with a proper morphism f¯:X→𝐀1\overline{f}\colon X\to{\bf A}^{1} extending ff, with the property that each fiber of ff is dense in the corresponding fiber of f¯\overline{f}. It is often singular.

Let E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} be the horizontal components of X∖𝐀2X\setminus{\bf A}^{2}, namely the irreducible components of X∖𝐀2X\setminus{\bf A}^{2} that dominate 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}. By standard results, E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} are isomorphic to 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} and do not intersect (Proposition 1). To each EiE_{i} we associate two integers. The first is the degree eie_{i} of EiE_{i} over 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}; one can think of e1,…,ere_{1},\ldots,e_{r} as the orders of the orbits of the monodromy group acting on the branches at infinity of a general fiber of ff. The second is the least positive integer δi\delta_{i} such that δi​Ei\delta_{i}E_{i} is a Cartier divisor on XX; since EiE_{i} is smooth, we have that δi=1\delta_{i}=1 if and only if XX has no singularities along EiE_{i}.

Our result (Theorem 1) says that if the characteristic of κ\kappa is 0, the greatest common divisor of δ1​e1,…,δr​er\delta_{1}e_{1},\ldots,\delta_{r}e_{r} is 1. In particular, if there only one component E1E_{1}, this maps isomorphically onto 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}, and f¯\overline{f} is smooth along E1E_{1}. So, if one of the fibers of ff has only one branch at infinity, then there is a simultaneous resolution of singularities at infinity of ff. This easily implies the Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh embedding theorem.

One can show that the integers ei​δie_{i}\delta_{i} coincide with the integers mim_{i} defined by Eisenbud and Neumann (see [AB], p. 102). So in characteristic 0 our result follows from [EN], section 4, although our proof is shorter.

In characteristic pp we only get that the greatest common divisor of δ1​e1,…,δr​er\delta_{1}e_{1},\ldots,\delta_{r}e_{r} is 1 when the degree of the polynomial is prime to pp (see Theorem 2). This implies the Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh embedding theorem over a perfect field.

The proof of the Theorem 1 is entirely straightforward, and very short; it uses standard topological methods, plus some elementary facts about rational surface singularities. If one substitutes ordinary topological cohomology with étale cohomology with 𝐙ℓ{\bf Z}_{\ell} coefficients, where ℓ\ell is a prime different from the characteristic of κ\kappa, one gets a proof of Theorem 2. We do not include the proof of this general case, but anyone who is familiar with étale cohomology will be able to reconstruct the details.

3 The results

Consider a complex polynomial in two variables, i.e., a morphism f:𝐀2→𝐀1f\colon{\bf A}^{2}\to{\bf A}^{1} defined over C. We shall always assume that ff is primitive, that is, that ff is not constant, and not obtained by composition with a polynomial in one variable of degree greater than 1. This the same as saying that the generic fiber of ff is integral, or that the subfield 𝐂⁡(f){\bf C}(f) is algebraically closed in 𝐂⁡(x,y){\bf C}(x,y).

We consider the minimal normal compactification f¯:X→𝐀1\overline{f}\colon X\to{\bf A}^{1} of ff, obtained by taking the closure Γ\Gamma of the graph of ff in 𝐏2×𝐏1{\bf P}^{2}\times{\bf P}^{1}, considering its normalization X′X^{\prime}, and then calling XX the inverse image of 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} in X′X^{\prime}. Then XX is a normal integral complex quasiprojective scheme over κ\kappa, containing 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} as an open subscheme. Furthermore the morphism ff extends to a morphism f¯:X→𝐀1\overline{f}\colon X\to{\bf A}^{1}, which has the useful property that every fiber of ff is dense inside the corresponding fiber of f¯\overline{f}. Let us call E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} the irreducible components of the complement EE of 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} in XX. Each of the E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} is an affine integral curve dominating 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}: we will call e1,…,ere_{1},\ldots,e_{r} the degrees of E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} over 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}.

Furthermore, the divisor class groups of the local rings of XX are finite, because XX has rational singularities ([Li], Proposition 17.1.) We will call δi\delta_{i} the least common multiple of the orders of EiE_{i} in each of the divisor class groups of the local rings of XX at points of EiE_{i}; clearly δi​Ei\delta_{i}E_{i} is a Cartier divisor on XX, while δ​Ei\delta E_{i} is not a Cartier divisor for any integer δ\delta with 0<δ<δi0<\delta<\delta_{i}.

Theorem 1.  Each of the E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} is isomorphic to 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}, and they are pairwise disjoint.

Furthermore the greatest common divisor of the products δ1​e1,…,δr​er\delta_{1}e_{1},\ldots,\delta_{r}e_{r} is 1.

The first statement in the theorem is quite standard. It has an important consequence; if δi\delta_{i} is 1, that is, if EiE_{i} is a Cartier divisor on XX, then XX is smooth at all point of EiE_{i}.

Corollary 1.  Assume that XX has only one component at infinity. Then all the fibers of f¯\overline{f} are integral and smooth at infinity.

In particular, this happens when one of the fibers of ff has only one branch at infinity.

This follows immediately from the theorem, because the hypothesis implies that δ1=1\delta_{1}=1, i.e., XX is smooth, and e1=1e_{1}=1, i.e., E1E_{1} maps isomorphically onto 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}.

From the corollary we get a new proof of the renowned Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh theorem. For this we only need to assume that κ\kappa is perfect.

The Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh theorem over C.  Any embedding of 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} into 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} defined over C is equivalent to the standard embedding t↦(t,0)t\mapsto(t,0).

Proof. . Let CC be a curve in 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} isomorphic to 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}, f∈𝐂⁡[x,y]f\in{\bf C}[x,y] a generator of the ideal of CC. Because of the corollary, each geometric fiber of f¯\overline{f} is isomorphic to 𝐏1{\bf P}^{1}, so XX is a 𝐏1{\bf P}^{1}-bundle on 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}. If we call EE the complement of 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} in XX, with its reduced scheme structure, then the projection from EE onto 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} is an isomorphism. Hence there is an isomorphism ϕ\phi of 𝐏1×𝐀1{\bf P}^{1}\times{\bf A}^{1} with XX carrying 𝐀1×∞{\bf A}^{1}\times{\infty} into EE, and such that f¯∘ϕ:𝐏1×𝐀1→𝐀1\overline{f}\circ\phi\colon{\bf P}^{1}\times{\bf A}^{1}\to{\bf A}^{1} is the second projection. The restriction of ϕ\phi to 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} carries the line with equation y=0y=0 into CC, and this proves the theorem.   ♣\clubsuit

This can be made to work in positive characteristic. Let us fix an algebraically closed field κ\kappa, and call pp be the characteristic exponent of κ\kappa, namely the characteristic of κ\kappa if this is positive, and 1 otherwise.

Consider a primitive polynomial in two variables, i.e., a morphism f:𝐀2→𝐀1f\colon{\bf A}^{2}\to{\bf A}^{1} defined over κ\kappa with integral general fiber; as before, ff has a minimal normal compactification f¯:X→𝐀1\overline{f}\colon X\to{\bf A}^{1}. Define E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r}, e1,…,ere_{1},\ldots,e_{r} and δ1,…,δr\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{r} as before. Then we can not conclude that the δi​ei\delta_{i}e_{i} are relatively prime; however, we have the following.

Theorem 2.  Each of the E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} is isomorphic to 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}, and they are pairwise disjoint.

Furthermore the greatest common divisor of the products δ1​e1,…,δr​er\delta_{1}e_{1},\ldots,\delta_{r}e_{r} is a power of pp and divides the degree of ff.

We still get the corollary, in the following form.

Corollary 2.  Assume that the degree of ff is prime to the pp, and that XX has only one component at infinity. Then all the fibers of f¯\overline{f} are integral and smooth at infinity.

In particular, this happens when one of the fibers of ff has only one branch at infinity.

Remarkably, using a different technique one can prove that XX is smooth when it has only one component at infinity, without assuming that the degree of ff is prime to pp. Unfortunately, I do not have any interesting application of this.

From Corollary 2 we get a new proof of the Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh theorem over any perfect field.

The Suzuki–Abhyankar–Moh theorem over a perfect field.  Any embedding of 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} into 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} defined over a perfect field, whose degree is relatively prime to the characteristic of κ\kappa is equivalent to the standard embedding t↦(t,0)t\mapsto(t,0).

Proof of Theorem 1. Recall that Γ\Gamma is the closure of the graph of ff in 𝐏2×𝐏1{\bf P}^{2}\times{\bf P}^{1}, X′X^{\prime} its normalization, f′f^{\prime} and π\pi the projections of X′X^{\prime} onto 𝐏1{\bf P}^{1} and 𝐏2{\bf P}^{2}, respectively. Let L=𝐏2∖𝐀2L={\bf P}^{2}\setminus{\bf A}^{2} be the line at infinity, L′L^{\prime} its proper transform in X′X^{\prime}.

Let Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} be the closure of EiE_{i} in X′X^{\prime}: the first statement of the theorem is a consequence of the following fact.

Lemma 1.  The curves L′L^{\prime} and Ei′E^{\prime}_{i}, for each i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r, are isomorphic to 𝐏1{\bf P}^{1}, and any two of them do not intersect in more than one point. Furthermore, if Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} and Ej′E^{\prime}_{j}, with i≠ji\neq j, intersect in a closed point p∈X′p\in X^{\prime}, then p∈L′p\in L^{\prime}.

Assuming Lemma 1, and keeping in mind that that L′L^{\prime} is the fiber of f′f^{\prime} over the point at infinity ∞∈𝐏1​(κ)\infty\in{\bf P}^{1}(\kappa), we see that each of the Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} can have only one point over ∞\infty, and therefore the inverse image EiE_{i} of 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} in Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} is isomorphic to 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1}. Also from Lemma 1 we get that the EiE_{i} do not intersect.

Proof. The natural morphism π:X′→𝐏2\pi\colon X^{\prime}\to{\bf P}^{2} is birational and 𝐏2{\bf P}^{2} is smooth, so R1​π∗​𝒪X′=0{\rm R}^{1}\pi_{*}{\cal O}_{X^{\prime}}=0. Let L~=π−1​(L)red\widetilde{L}=\pi^{-1}(L)_{\rm red}. Since 𝒪L~{\cal O}_{\widetilde{L}} is a quotient of 𝒪X′{\cal O}_{X^{\prime}}, so R1​π∗​𝒪L~=0{\rm R}^{1}\pi_{*}{\cal O}_{\widetilde{L}}=0. We have π∗​𝒪L~=𝒪L\pi_{*}{\cal O}_{\widetilde{L}}={\cal O}_{L}, so from the Leray spectral sequence

E2i​j=Hi​(𝐏1,Rj​π∗​𝒪L~)⟹Hi+j​(L~,𝒪)E_{2}^{ij}={\rm H}^{i}({\bf P}^{1},{\rm R}^{j}\pi_{*}{\cal O}_{\widetilde{L}})\Longrightarrow{\rm H}^{i+j}(\widetilde{L},{\cal O})

we get that H1​(L~,𝒪)=0{\rm H}^{1}(\widetilde{L},{\cal O})=0. If ZZ is subscheme of L~\widetilde{L}, the sheaf 𝒪Z{\cal O}_{Z} is a quotient of 𝒪π−1​(L){\cal O}_{\pi^{-1}(L)}, and if ℐ{\cal I} is the ideal of ZZ in π−1​(L)\pi^{-1}(L) we have H2​(π−1​(L),ℐ)=0{\rm H}^{2}(\pi^{-1}(L),{\cal I})=0, hence H1​(Z,𝒪)=0{\rm H}^{1}(Z,{\cal O})=0. This in particular applies to any of the curves L′L^{\prime} and Ei′E^{\prime}_{i}. Any integral projective curve with arithmetic genus 0 is isomorphic to 𝐏1{\bf P}^{1}.

Also, if C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are two of these curve, from the fact that H1​(C1∪C2,𝒪)=0{\rm H}^{1}(C_{1}\cup C_{2},{\cal O})=0 we see that C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} have at most one common point. Analogously, the fact that H1​(L′∪Ei′∪Ej′,𝒪)=0{\rm H}^{1}(L^{\prime}\cup E^{\prime}_{i}\cup E^{\prime}_{j},{\cal O})=0 implies that Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} and Ej′E^{\prime}_{j} cannot meet outside of L′L^{\prime}, because L′L^{\prime} meets both Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} and Ej′E^{\prime}_{j}.   ♣\clubsuit

Now consider the group PicX\mathop{\rm Pic}X of Cartier divisors on XX, and the natural map PicX→ClX\mathop{\rm Pic}X\to\mathop{\rm Cl}X into the group of Weil divisors. Since 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2} is factorial, and all of its invertible regular functions are constant, it follows that ClX\mathop{\rm Cl}X is a free abelian group with basis E1E_{1}, …, ErE_{r}. Since the map PicX→ClX\mathop{\rm Pic}X\to\mathop{\rm Cl}X is injective, because XX is normal, this proves the following.

Lemma 2.  The group PicX\mathop{\rm Pic}X is free, with basis δ1​E1\delta_{1}E_{1}, …, δr​Er\delta_{r}E_{r}.

The fact that the δi​ei\delta_{i}e_{i} are relatively prime is easily proved, after having established the following two facts.

Lemma 3.  The first Chern class map PicX→H2​(X,𝐙)\mathop{\rm Pic}X\to{\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z}) is an isomorphism.

Lemma 4.  Let CC be a general fiber of f¯\overline{f}. The the restriction map H2​(X,𝐙)→H2​(C,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\rm H}^{2}(C,{\bf Z}) is surjective.

In fact, the restriction of δi​Ei\delta_{i}E_{i} to CC has degree δi​ei\delta_{i}e_{i}; the three lemmas together imply that the restriction of the δi​Ei\delta_{i}E_{i} generate H2​(C,𝐙)=𝐙{\rm H}^{2}(C,{\bf Z})={\bf Z}, hence that 1 is a linear combination of the δi​ei\delta_{i}e_{i}.

There remains to give proofs of the last two lemmas; both are rather formal.

Proof of Lemma 3. Let ρ:X~→X\rho\colon\widetilde{X}\to X be a resolution of the singularities of XX, F1,…,FsF_{1},\ldots,F_{s} the exceptional divisors, E~i\widetilde{E}_{i} the proper transforms of the EiE_{i}. Then the complement of the FjF_{j} and the E~i\widetilde{E}_{i} in X~\widetilde{X} is 𝐀2{\bf A}^{2}; therefore the Picard group of X~\widetilde{X} is freely generated by the FjF_{j} and the E~i\widetilde{E}_{i}. Likewise, H2​(X~,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) is freely generated by the cohomology classes of the EiE_{i} and FjF_{j}; so the first Chern class map PicX~→H2​(X~,𝐙)\mathop{\rm Pic}\widetilde{X}\to{\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) is an isomorphism.

The pullback map PicX→PicX~\mathop{\rm Pic}X\to\mathop{\rm Pic}\widetilde{X} is clearly injective, and a divisor class in PicX~\mathop{\rm Pic}\widetilde{X} is in the image of PicX\mathop{\rm Pic}X if and only if its restriction to each of the FjF_{j} has degree 0. The reason is that XX has rational singularities ([Li], Theorem 12.1

Now take cohomology. We have that R1​ρ∗​𝐙X~=0{\rm R}^{1}\rho_{*}{\bf Z}_{\widetilde{X}}=0, while ρ∗​𝐙X~=𝐙\rho_{*}{\bf Z}_{\widetilde{X}}={\bf Z}, and R2​ρ∗​𝐙X~{\rm R}^{2}\rho_{*}{\bf Z}_{\widetilde{X}} is a sheaf concentrated in the singular points of XX, whose stalk over p∈Xp\in X is a direct sum of one copy of Z for each exceptional divisor over pp. By considering the Leray spectral sequence of the map ρ:X~→X\rho\colon\widetilde{X}\to X, one deduces that the restriction map H2​(X,𝐙)→H2​(X~,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) is injective, and its image consists exactly of the classes in H2​(X~,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) which have degree 0 on each FjF_{j}.

By putting these two statements together, we see that PicX\mathop{\rm Pic}X and H2​(X,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z}) are identified with two subgroups of PicX~\mathop{\rm Pic}\widetilde{X} and H2​(X~,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) which correspond under the isomorphism PicX~→H2​(X~,𝐙)\mathop{\rm Pic}\widetilde{X}\to{\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z}) given by the first Chern class. This proves Lemma 3.   ♣\clubsuit

Proof of Lemma 4. Consider the Leray spectral sequence

E2i​j=Hi​(𝐀1,Rj​f¯∗​𝐙X)⟹Hi+j​(X,𝐙);E_{2}^{ij}={\rm H}^{i}\bigl({\bf A}^{1},{\rm R}^{j}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X}\bigr)\Longrightarrow{\rm H}^{i+j}(X,{\bf Z});

since H2​(𝐀1,R1​f¯∗​𝐙X)=0{\rm H}^{2}\bigl({\bf A}^{1},{\rm R}^{1}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X}\bigr)=0, because 𝐀1{\bf A}^{1} is an affine curve and R1​f¯∗​𝐙X{\rm R}^{1}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X} a constructible sheaf, we get that the map

H2​(X,𝐙)→H0​(𝐀1,R2​f¯∗​𝐙X){\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\rm H}^{0}({\bf A}^{1},{\rm R}^{2}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X})

is surjective. Now take the trace map

tr:R2​f¯∗​𝐙X→𝐙𝐀1.\mathop{\rm tr}:{\rm R}^{2}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X}\to{\bf Z}_{{\bf A}^{1}}.

Because the general fiber of f¯\overline{f} is integral, the trace map is generically an isomorphism. Let F=f¯−1​(t)F=\overline{f}^{-1}(t) be a fiber of f¯\overline{f} over a closed point t∈𝐀1​(κ)t\in{\bf A}^{1}(\kappa), F1,…,FsF_{1},\ldots,F_{s} the irreducible components of FF, m1,…,msm_{1},\ldots,m_{s} the lengths of the local rings of FF at F1,…,FsF_{1},\ldots,F_{s}. By proper base change the stalk (R2​f¯∗​𝐙X)t\bigl({\rm R}^{2}\overline{f}_{*}{\bf Z}_{X})_{t} is canonically isomorphic to

H2​(F,𝐙)≃⨁i=1sH2​(Fi,𝐙)≃𝐙s;{\rm H}^{2}(F,{\bf Z})\simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}{\rm H}^{2}(F_{i},{\bf Z})\simeq{\bf Z}^{s};

with this identification, the trace map on the stalks over t∈𝐀1​(κ)t\in{\bf A}^{1}(\kappa) is identified with the map from 𝐙s{\bf Z}^{s} to Z that sends (k1,…,ks)(k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}) to k1​m1+⋯+ks​msk_{1}m_{1}+\cdots+k_{s}m_{s}. But m1,⋯,msm_{1},\cdots,m_{s} are relatively prime, because f:S→𝐀1f\colon S\to{\bf A}^{1} does not have multiple fibers, so the trace map is surjective, and its kernel is concentrated on a finite number of points. By taking global sections we see that the global trace map

tr:H2​(X,𝐙)→𝐙\mathop{\rm tr}:{\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\bf Z}

is surjective. But tr:H2​(X,𝐙)→𝐙\mathop{\rm tr}:{\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\bf Z} coincides with the restriction map H2​(X,𝐙)→H2​(C,𝐙)≃𝐙{\rm H}^{2}(X,{\bf Z})\to{\rm H}^{2}(C,{\bf Z})\simeq{\bf Z}. Hence this restriction map is surjective. This proves the lemma, and hence the theorem.   ♣\clubsuit

Note.  From the spectral sequence of the map X→𝐀1X\to{\bf A}^{1} one deduces that H3​(X,𝐙)=0{\rm H}^{3}(X,{\bf Z})=0; furthermore, from the spectral sequence of a resolution X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X one sees that the restriction map H2​(X~,𝐙)→H2​(F,𝐙){\rm H}^{2}(\widetilde{X},{\bf Z})\to{\rm H}^{2}(F,{\bf Z}) is surjective. From this one can deduce that the class of EiE_{i} generates the product ∏p∈EiCl𝒪^X,p\prod_{p\in E_{i}}\mathop{\rm Cl}\widehat{\cal O}_{X,p}; this means that δi\delta_{i} can also be defined as the product of the orders of the group Cl𝒪^X,p\mathop{\rm Cl}\widehat{\cal O}_{X,p} for p∈Eip\in E_{i}.

To prove Theorem 2 one follows the steps in the proof of Theorem 1, subsituting étale cohomology with 𝐙ℓ{\bf Z}_{\ell} coefficients to classical cohomology, where ℓ\ell is a prime different from the characteristic of κ\kappa; in this way one shows that ℓ\ell does not divide the greatest common divisor of the ei​δie_{i}\delta_{i}. We leave the details to the interested reader. The only thing that does not follow is that the greatest common divisor of the δi​ei\delta_{i}e_{i} divides the degree dd of ff.

To show this, call CC the closure in 𝐏2{\bf P}^{2} of a general fiber of ff, C′C^{\prime} the proper transform of CC in X′X^{\prime}. Then C′C^{\prime} is a general fiber of f′f^{\prime}, hence it is a Cartier divisor on X′X^{\prime}; the intersection number (C′⋅L′)(C^{\prime}\cdot L^{\prime}) is 0, and (C′⋅Ei′)=ei(C^{\prime}\cdot E^{\prime}_{i})=e_{i} for each i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. We have a decomposition of π∗​(L)\pi^{*}(L) as a Weil divisor

π∗​[L]=[L′]+∑i=1rmi​Ei\pi^{*}[L]=[L^{\prime}]+\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}

for certain positive integers m1,…,mrm_{1},\ldots,m_{r}. Since the restriction of the mi​Eim_{i}E_{i} to XX must be a Cartier divisor, we see that δi\delta_{i} divides mim_{i}, so we write

π∗​[L]=[L′]+∑i=1rni​δi​Ei.\pi^{*}[L]=[L^{\prime}]+\sum_{i=1}^{r}n_{i}\delta_{i}E_{i}.

But

d=(C⋅L)=(C′⋅π∗​[L])=(C′⋅L′)+∑i=1rni​δi​(C′⋅Ei′)=∑i=1rni​δi​ei,d=(C\cdot L)=(C^{\prime}\cdot\pi^{*}[L])=(C^{\prime}\cdot L^{\prime})+\sum_{i=1}^{r}n_{i}\delta_{i}(C^{\prime}\cdot E^{\prime}_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{r}n_{i}\delta_{i}e_{i},

by the projection formula, and this completes the proof.   ♣\clubsuit

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
